translations.text: The words of the Ecclesiastes (the Preacher), son of David, king of Israel, in Jerusalem.
"Vanity of vanities," said the Ecclesiastes, "vanity of vanities, all is vanity."
What advantage does a man have in all his toil with which he toils under the sun?
A generation passes away and a generation comes, and the earth endures.
And the sun rises and the sun sets, and it goes to its place.
It rises, and goes there to the south and turns round to the north; the wind goes round about, and the wind returns on its circuit.
All the torrents flow into the sea, and the sea is filled [?]. To the place where the torrents go, there they return again to go.
All words are wearisome; a man is not able to speak them, nor is the eye satisfied with seeing, nor is the ear filled with hearing.
What is it that has been made? The very same as that which will be; and there is nothing at all new under this sun.
Concerning which someone would speak and say, "This is new" — it was already made long ago, in the ages that were before us.
There is no remembrance of the first and of the last, who were before us; there is no remembrance of them among those things that are made last.
I, the Ecclesiastes, was king over Israel in Jerusalem.

And I gave my heart to seek out and to consider by wisdom all things that are done under this sun; for He has given a distracting business of toil to the sons of men, that they should be distracted in it.
I saw all things altogether that are done under this sun, and behold, all is vanity and a choosing of wind.
That which is crooked cannot be set right, and that which is lacking cannot be counted.

I spoke in my heart and said: "Behold, I have become greater than those who were before me in Jerusalem, and I have increased in wisdom beyond all who were before me in Jerusalem"; and my heart saw much wisdom and knowledge.
I came to know parables and understanding, for this too is a choosing of wind.
For in the abundance of wisdom is abundance of knowledge, and whoever increases knowledge increases pain.
I said in my heart: "Come now, and I will test you with joy; and look upon what is good." And this too was vanity.
To laughter I said, "Distraction!" and to joy, "What are you doing?"

And I considered in my heart to draw on my heart as with wine, while my heart guided me in wisdom, and to lay hold of merriment, until I should see what is good for the sons of men, which they should do under this sun for the number of the days of their life.
I made great my works; I built myself houses and planted myself vineyards.
I made myself gardens and orchards, and planted in them every kind of fruit-bearing tree.
And I made myself pools of water, to water from them the groves of growing trees.
I acquired male and female slaves, and I had servants born in my house; and my possessions of herds and flocks were very great, greater than those of all who were before me in Jerusalem.
I gathered for myself both gold and silver, and the treasures of kings and of lands. I got myself male and female singers as delights for the sons of men, and male and female cupbearers.
And I became great, and I gained more than all who were before me in Jerusalem, and my wisdom stayed with me.
And whatever my eyes asked for, I did not keep back from them. I did not keep my heart back from any joy, for my heart rejoiced in all my labour, and this was my portion from all my labour.

And I looked at all my works that my hands had made, and at the toil I had toiled at to do them. And behold, all is vanity and a chasing of the spirit, and there is nothing to be gained under the sun.
And I turned to look at wisdom, and at luxury and joy. For who is the man who will come after, following the track of his own counsel, in all that he has done?
And I saw that wisdom has more advantage than folly, as light has more advantage than darkness.
The wise man's eyes are in his head, and the fool walks in darkness. And I also knew that one fate befalls them all.

And I said in my heart, "As the fate of the fool is, the same fate will befall me too. Why then did I become wiser?" I said this firmly in my heart: "This too is vanity," for the fool speaks out of the excess of his heart.
For the wise man is remembered no more than the fool, for ever, since in the days to come everything is already forgotten. And how does the wise man die along with the fool?
And I hated my whole life, for the work that is done under this sun is grievous to me, for all is vanity and a choosing of the spirit.
And I hated all my toil that I labour at under this sun, for I will leave it to the man who comes after me.

And who knows whether he will be wise or foolish? Yet he will have power over all the fruit of my labour, all that I laboured for and all that I gained by my wisdom under this sun. This too is vanity.
And I turned to separate my heart from all the labour that I had laboured at under this sun.
For there is a man whose labour is done with wisdom, knowledge and courage, and to a man who did not labour for it he will give it as his portion. This too is vanity and a great evil.
For what does this man have from all his labour, and from the choosing of his heart, that he labours at under this sun?
For all his days are full of pain and vexation and anxious distraction, and even at night his heart does not sleep. This too is vanity.
There is nothing good for a man in all his labour
except to eat and drink and show his soul good, good in his labour. And I saw this too, that it is from the hand of God. For who will eat and drink without him?

For to the man [?] before his face he has given wisdom and knowledge, and to the sinner he has given busy toil, to gather and to give to the one who is good before the face of God. For this too is vanity and a chasing of the spirit.
For everything there is a time, and there is a time for every matter under heaven.
There is a time to be born and a time to die; there is a time to plant and a time to uproot what was planted;
there is a time to kill and a time to heal; there is a time to tear down and a time to build up.
A time for weeping and a time for laughing, a time for mourning and a time for dancing.
There is a time to lay down stones and a time to gather stones; there is a time for embracing and a time to separate from the one embraced.
There is a time for seeking and a time for losing; there is a time for keeping and a time for casting away;
there is a time for tearing and a time for sewing; there is a time for silence and a time for speaking;
there is a time for love and a time for hatred; there is a time for war and a time for peace.
What advantage does the worker have in that over which he toils?
I saw all the distraction that God has given to the sons of men, so that they might be distracted by it.
He made everything good in its time; he also put all eternity into their heart, so that a man may not find out the work of God which God has done from the beginning to the end.
I understood that there is nothing good among these things except that one should rejoice and do good in his life.
And for every man who eats and drinks and sees good in all his toil, this is a gift of God.
I knew that everything God has made will remain forever; nothing can be added to it and nothing can be taken away from it; and God has made it so that people should fear before his face.
What has been already was long ago, and whatever has been is what will be; it has already been done; and God will seek out what has been pursued.
And again I saw under this sun the place of judgment, and there was the ungodly man; and the place of the righteous, and there was the godly man.
And I said in my heart: "Will God judge the righteous and the ungodly? For there is a time for every matter and for every deed."
There I said in my heart concerning the speech of the sons of men: "God will judge them and show that they are beasts."

For the fate of the sons of men is like the fate of the beast; they have one fate: as the one dies, so the other dies, and there is one breath in all of them. And in what does man surpass the beast? In nothing, for all is vanity.
And all go to one place; all were made from the earth and all return to the earth.
And who knows whether the spirit of the sons of men goes up above, and whether the spirit of beasts goes down into the earth?
And I saw that there is nothing good except that a man should rejoice in all his works, for that is his portion. For who can bring him to see what will be after him?

And I turned and saw all the oppressions that are done under this sun. And behold, the tears of the oppressors, and there is no one to comfort them; power is in the hand of the oppressors, and there is no one to comfort them.
And I praised the dead who have already died more than the living who are still alive.
And better than both of these is the one who has not yet been, who has not seen all this evil work that is done under heaven.
And I saw all the evil toil of the man who has made himself strong: it is a man's envy of his neighbour. This too is vanity and chasing after wind.
The fool folds his hands and eats up his own flesh.
Better is one handful full of rest than two handfuls full of toil and chasing after wind.
And I turned and saw vanity under this sun.

There is one, and there is no second; he has neither son nor brother. And there is no end to all his labor, and his eyes are not satisfied with wealth. And for whom do I toil and deprive my soul of good? And all this is vanity and an evil distraction.
Two are better than one, for they have a good reward; it is in his labor [?].
If they fall, the one will raise up his companion. But woe to the one who is alone, if he falls and there is no second to raise him up.
And if two lie down together, they become warm; but how will the one alone become warm?
And if one overpowers him, these two will stand against him; and a cord that is laid together [?] does not quickly snap.
Better is a servant who is poor and wise than an old and foolish king who did not know how to take heed.
For he came out of the prison house to reign, and in his kingdom he became poor.
I saw all the living who walk under the sun with that second youth, who stood up in his place.
There is no end to all the people, to all who were before them, and those who come after will not rejoice in him; for this too is vanity and a striving after wind.
Guard your foot when you go into the house of God, and draw near to listen rather than to give the sacrifice of fools, for they do not know how to do good.
Do not be hasty with your mouth, and do not let your heart hasten to bring forth a word before God, for God is in heaven and you are on earth. Therefore let your words be few,
for a dream comes with a multitude of trial [?], and the voice of a fool with a multitude of words.
When you have made a vow to God, do not delay to pay it; there is no pleasure among fools. Whatever you have vowed to give, give.
It is better for you not to vow than to vow and not pay.
Do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin, and do not say before the face of God, “It was ignorance,” lest God be angry at your voice and destroy the works of your hands.
For in many dreams there are also vanities and many words; but you, fear God.
If you see the oppression of the poor and the robbing of judgment and justice in the land, do not marvel at this matter; for a high one watches over the high one, and higher ones are over them.
And the advantage of the land is over all; he himself is the king of that field of yours. And be faithful in everything; [?] it is heavy, that distraction [?].
Whoever loves silver will not be satisfied with silver; and who has loved fruit in its abundance [?]? This too is vanity.
When good things increase, those who eat them increase; and then again, what strength is there with him [?], except the beginning of seeing with his eyes [?].
Sweet is the sleep of a servant, whether he eats little or much; but being satisfied and growing rich [?] — there is no one who lets him sleep [?].
There is a sickness that I saw under this sun: wealth kept by its owner to his own harm.
And that wealth perishes through evil distraction; he has fathered a son, and there is nothing in his hands, not one thing.
As he came forth naked from his mother's womb, so he returns to go back there, to the earth, as he came; and he will carry away nothing from his labor in his hand when he departs.
And this too is an evil sickness: as he came, so shall he go. And what more is there for the one who toils in vain?
And all his days are spent in darkness and mourning, and in much anger, sickness and sorrow.

Behold, I have seen one thing that is good: to eat and to drink and to see good in all the labor that a man labors under this sun, through the numbered days of the life that God has given him, for that is his portion.
And every man to whom God has given wealth and possessions, and whom he has enabled to take his portion of them and eat of them: this is the gift of God.
For the days of his life will not be much remembered, because God has kept him occupied with the joy of his heart.
There is an evil that I have seen under this sun, and it is great among men:

a man to whom God has given wealth and produce and glory, so that his soul lacks nothing of all that his heart desired, and yet God has not enabled him to eat of it, for another man will eat it. This too is vanity and an evil sickness.

If a man begets a hundred children and lives many years, and the days of the years of his life are many, but his soul is not satisfied with good, and he does not even receive a burial, I said: "The stillborn child is better off than he,
for it came in vanity, and darkness will cover its name.
And it has not seen the sun or known anything; it has more rest than he does.
Even if he lived a thousand years many times over and saw no good, do not all go to one place?"
All the toil of a man is for his mouth, and yet the soul is not satisfied.
For the wise man has more than the fool, for the poor man knows how to walk before his life.
The sight of the eyes is better than a wandering soul. This too is vanity and a chasing after the wind.
Whatever has come into being, its name was called long ago, and what each thing is has been made known to men. And he cannot contend in judgment with one who is stronger than he.
For there are many words that increase vanity. But what advantage does a man have?
Or who knows what is good for him in his life, the numbered days of his vain life? And he spends them in shadow. And who will tell a man what will happen after him under this sun?
A house [?] is better than good mercy [?], and the day of death is better than the day of birth.
It is better to go into a house of mourning than to go into a house of feasting, for this is the end of every man, and the living will lay good to his heart.
Anger is better than laughter, for through a sad face the heart is made glad.
The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, and the heart of the fool is in the house of joy.
It is better to listen to the rebuke of a wise man than to be a man who listens to the entertainment of fools.
Like the sound of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of fools. This too is vanity.
For slander shakes the wise man and destroys his steadfast heart.
The last word is better than the first; a patient man is better than a proud spirit.
Do not be quick in your spirit to grow angry, for anger rests in the bosom of fools.
Do not say, "Why is it that the former days were better than these?" For you have not asked this out of wisdom.
Therefore wisdom is good along with an inheritance, and it is an advantage to those who see the sun.
For its shadow is under wisdom, like the shadow of silver, and the advantage of wisdom gives life through it.
Look at the works of God: who is able to set in order what God has overturned?
In the days of good, live well, and in the evil day, look; see that this too is set alongside those. God did this for the sake of the word, so that after him a person might find nothing at all.
I have seen everything in the days of my vanity: a righteous man is not lost in his righteousness, and there is an ungodly man who lives on and stands firm in his wickedness.
Do not be overly righteous, and do not be wise beyond measure, so that you do not falter.
Do not be overly ungodly, and do not be harsh, so that you do not die before your time.
It is good for you to take this upon yourself, in this matter, and do not let it make your hand defiled, for the one who fears God will come through all of this.
Wisdom helps a man more than ten rulers who were in the city.
For there is no righteous man on earth who has done good and has not sinned.
Do not take to heart all the words that the ungodly speak, so that you do not hear your servant cursing you.
For many times he will do wickedness to you, and many times he will do evil to your soul, just as you cursed others.
All this I tested by wisdom, and I said, "I have become wise."
But it moved far away from me, farther than before; and the depth of the deep, who can find it?
I went around, I and my heart, to know, to consider and to understand wisdom and the reckoning, and to perceive the folly of the ungodly, their turmoil and their being carried this way and that.

And I found it, and I said: "More bitter than death is the woman who is a huntress; her heart is a snare and her hands are fetters." The one who is good before God will escape from her, but the sinner is caught by her.
"Behold, this I have found," said the Preacher, "adding one thing to another to find the reasonings
that my soul sought, and I did not find them. One man out of a thousand I found, but a woman among all these I did not find.
Behold, this I have found: God made man upright, but they have sought out many schemes."
Who knows the wise? And who knows the interpretation of words? A man's wisdom makes his face shine, and one with a shameless face will be hated.
Keep the command of the king, and do not be hasty on account of the word of the oath of God,
for you go before his face. Do not persist in an evil word, for whatever he wishes will be done.
For the king is sovereign, and who will say to him, "What are you doing?"
Whoever has kept the commandments will not know an evil word, and the heart of the wise knows the time of discernment.
For there is a time and a judgment for every matter, because a man's knowledge weighs heavily on him.
For he does not know what is going to happen, and who will tell him how it will be?
No man has power over the spirit, to hold back the spirit, and there is no power over the day of death, and there is no embassy in the day of battle, and the ungodly man will not deliver what is his.
I saw all this, and I gave my heart to every work that is done under this sun, in all the things where a man has power over another man to do him harm.
Then I saw the ungodly being carried into the grave, and some of the holy ones too. They went away, and they were [?] in the city, because they had done so. This too is vanity.
For no sentence comes quickly on those who do evil. Therefore the heart of the sons of men grew bold within them to do evil.
The one who sinned has done evil from that time on and from long before them. And I know this: it will go well for those who fear God, so that they may stand in fear before their face.
But it will not go well for the ungodly man, and his days will not be lengthened in the shadow, because he does not stand in fear before the face of God.
There is a vanity that is done on the earth: there are righteous people, and it happens to them as [?] the deed of the righteous. And I said, "This too is vanity."

So I praised joy, because nothing is good for a man under this sun except eating, drinking and merriment. This will stay with him in his labours through all the days of his life that God has given him under this sun.
During those days I gave my heart to know wisdom and to see the distraction and the care that are done on the earth, for day and night his eye does not see sleep.

I saw the whole work of God, and that a man cannot find out the work that is done under this sun. However hard a man strives to seek, he will not find it. And however much a wise man says he will know it, he is not able to find it.
For I laid all this to my heart, and my heart saw all this: that the righteous and the wise, and their works, are in the hand of God. And also love [?] man knows [?]; everything is before their face.

There is vanity in everything. One fate befalls the righteous and the ungodly, the good and the evil, the pure and the impure, the one who offers sacrifice and the one who does not. As with the good man, so with the sinner; as with the one who swears falsely, so with the one who fears an oath.

This is an evil in all the things that are done under this sun: one fate befalls everyone. The heart of the sons of men is also filled with evil, and distraction is in their heart while they live, and after that they go to the dead.
And who is there who will have a share? For all the living there is hope, because a living dog is better than a dead lion.
Their love and their hatred have perished as well, and they will never again have a portion in any of the works done under this sun.
Come, eat your bread with love and drink your wine with a merry heart, for the Lord has been pleased with your works.
Let your clothes be white at all times, and do not let your head lack oil.

And see life with the wife whom you have loved, all the days of your life that are given to you under this sun, all the days of your number. For this is your portion in your life and in the labours you toil at under this sun.
Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with all your strength. For there is no work, no counsel and no wisdom in hell, where you are going.

I turned and saw under this sun that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, nor bread to the wise, nor wealth to the understanding, nor favour to those with knowledge. For time and chance happen to them all.
For a man does not know his time. Fish are caught in an evil net, and birds are taken in a snare; in the same way the sons of men are snared in an evil time, when it falls on them suddenly.
And I also saw this: wisdom under this sun, and it seemed great to me.
There is a small city with few men in it. A great king comes against it, surrounds it and builds a great wall around it.
In it is found a poor and wise man, and by his wisdom he saves that city. Yet no one remembered that poor man.
And I said: "Wisdom is better than strength, yet the poor man's wisdom is despised and his words are not listened to."
The words of the wise are heard with attentive hearing [?], more than the shout of a ruler in folly.
Wisdom is better than weapons of war, and through one sin much good is destroyed.
Dead flies spoil the preparation of fragrant oil. A word of wisdom is more precious than the great glory of the fool.
The heart of the wise man is at his right hand, and the heart of the fool is at his left.
And when the fool walks along the road, his heart is lacking, and whatever he plans is all wickedness.
If the spirit of the ruler rises against you, do not leave your place, for calm puts an end to very great sins.
There is an evil that I saw under this sun, which came forth as if unintentionally from the presence of the ruler.
The fool was set, was set in very high places, and the rich sat in a low place.
I saw slaves on horses, and princes walking on foot on the ground like slaves.
Whoever digs a pit will fall into it himself, and whoever breaks through a wall will be bitten by a snake.
Whoever quarries stones will suffer from them, and whoever cuts wood will be endangered by it.
If the iron falls off, it has dulled the edge [?], and he must put in more strength. Is wisdom a man's advantage or not?
If a snake bites when it has not been charmed, then the charmer [?] has no advantage.
The words from the mouth of the wise are gracious, but the fool's lips swallow him up.
The beginning of the words of his mouth is folly, and the end of it is evil madness.
And the fool multiplies words. A man does not know what has been or what has been done. And who will tell him what will be after him?
The labour of fools will bring harm to the one who did not know how to go into the city.
Woe to you, O city, for your king is a youth, and your princes eat at dawn.
Blessed are you, O land, whose king is the son of a nobleman, and your princes eat at the proper time.
Through sloth the roofs sink low, and through idleness of the hands the house leaks.
They make bread for laughter, and wine and oil for the joy of the living, and everything submits to silver.
But do not curse the king even in your mind, and do not curse the rich man in the inner rooms of your bedchamber, for a bird will carry your voice, and that which has wings will tell your words.
Send out your bread upon the face of the water; after many days you will find it.
Give a portion to seven and also to eight, for you do not know what evil will come upon the earth.
If the clouds are filled with rain, they pour it out upon the earth; and if a tree falls to the south or to the north, in the place where the tree falls, there it will stay.
He who watches the rain does not sow, and he who looks at the clouds does not reap.
Just as one does not know what the way of the spirit is, like the bones in a pregnant womb, so they cannot know the works of God, all that he has made in all things.
In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening do not let your hand rest, for you do not know which will last, this or that, and if both alike, it is good.
And light is sweet, and it is good for the eyes to see the sun.
Even if a man lives many years and rejoices in all of them, let him remember the days of darkness, for they will be many. All that comes is vanity.

Rejoice, young man, in your youth, and let your heart gladden you in the days of your youth, and walk in your ways blamelessly, and not by the sight of your eyes. And understand that for all these things God will bring you into judgment.
And remove anger from your heart, and cast away wickedness from your flesh, for youth and folly are vanity.
And remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the days of evil come and the years draw near in which you will say, "I have no pleasure in them";
when the sun and the light and the moon and the stars grow dark, and the clouds return after the rain;

on the day when the keepers of the house tremble, and the men of strength are overturned, and the grinders are withdrawn because they have become few, and those who look out through the windows are darkened;
and they shut the doors on the streets because the sound of the grinder grows weak, and one rises up at the voice of the sparrow, and the daughters of song are brought low;

and they look out from on high, and there are terrors [?] in the way, and the almond tree blossoms, the locust grows fat, and the caper fails, for man has gone to his eternal home, and the mourners have gone about the streets;
before the silver cord is turned back, and the golden [?] (literally "colour") is shattered, and the pitcher is broken at the spring, and the wheel is shattered at the pit.
And the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God, who gave it.
"Vanity of vanities," said the Preacher, "all is vanity."
And besides this, because the Preacher was wise, he taught people knowledge, and he searched out many fine parables.
The Preacher searched hard to find pleasing words and upright writings.
The words of the wise are like a goad for an ox, and like heated nails, which were given from one shepherd; and more than these:
My son, beware of acquiring many books; there is no discipline and no completion in it, only much toil of the flesh. The end of the word:
Hear all this: fear God and keep his commandments, for this is for every man,
for God will bring every deed into judgment, every overlooked thing, whether good or whether evil.
